paternal responsiveness is associated with but not mediated by neophobia and anxiety-like behavior in biparental California mice (Peromyces californicus).

paternal behavior in male California mice is not associated with reduced anxiety or neural stress responsiveness, but is associated with reduced neophobia.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
paternal behavior is not facilitated by a decrease in neophobia and anxiety-like behavior, but rather is associated with these behaviors.
the transition from being an isolated virgin to a new father is not characterized by a reduction in anxiety, but is associated with increased anxiety-related behavior and neophobia.
paternal responsiveness in male California mice is associated with, rather than mediated by, reduced neophobia, anxiety-related behavior, and neural stress responsiveness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the onset of paternal responsiveness does not involve the same neurobiological mechanisms associated with the onset of maternal responsiveness.
paternal and maternal care are not associated with similar neural changes in male California mice.
the transition from being a virgin to being a father does not involve a reduction in anxiety, stress, or neophobia.
